title: How Drag Queens Work
summary: Josh Clark and Chuck Bryant, both in drag, discuss the history and culture of drag queens, based on a Kristen Conger article. They cover Julian Eltinge as a early "father of drag," the history of men playing women's roles from ancient Greece through Shakespeare's era, the Restoration ban and reopening of the stage to women, pantomime (panto), vaudeville drag, the gay bar and prohibition era, 1950s New York anti-cross-dressing law, the 1960s Mother Camp book, the Stonewall riots, Jose Julio Sarria's Imperial Court System, the Cockettes, drag preparation (shaving, makeup, hands, tucking with a gaff or tape, silicone breasts), drag names, drag performance jobs, Priscilla Queen of the Desert, and notable drag performers such as Mae West, RuPaul, Danny La Rue, Divine, Dame Edna, and Lady Bunny. The episode ends with a listener mail segment answering Owen's question about post-college career advice, and a sign-off.

segments.title: Opening banter in drag
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck, both in full drag, joke about their wigs, lashes, hands, and the gaff they use to tuck. They introduce the topic of drag queens and say the article is by Kristen Conger.

segments.title: Julian Eltinge and early drag stardom
segments.summary: The hosts describe Julian Eltinge (born William Dalton) as a considered father of drag in the early twentieth century. He performed in vaudeville, starred in The Fascinating Widow in 1911, worked in film, performed for King Edward VII, and was reportedly a lifelong bachelor who fought hecklers.

segments.title: Men playing women on stage through history
segments.summary: They trace men playing women's roles from ancient Greece, where women were barred from Greek drama, through the Middle Ages church pageants, to the 1660 decision by Charles II to let women on stage. Men playing women continued and became comic, leading to pantomime. Japanese kabuki went the other way, banning women and using onnagata performers into the nineteenth century.

segments.title: Pantomime, vaudeville, and fishy versus campy drag
segments.summary: The hosts explain pantomime (panto) as comedic drag in England, then describe American vaudeville touring shows, including family-friendly drag performances seen as good fun. They define fishy drag (aiming for femininity), campy drag (comedic), and glamour drag.

segments.title: Prohibition, early gay bars, and 1950s cross-dressing laws
segments.summary: Prohibition-era speakeasies gave gay men places to gather, leading to the first gay bars and later discos. San Francisco had a pansy craze. In the 1950s New York had a law requiring men in drag to wear at least three pieces of men's clothing. Drag shows at gay bars were affected.

segments.title: 1960s drag, female impersonators, and Stonewall
segments.summary: They cite Mother Camp's estimate of about five hundred regularly performing drag queens by the mid-1960s, and Jim Bailey's preference for the term illusionist or female impersonator. They discuss the origin of the term drag queen, then the June 1969 Stonewall riots at a mafia-run gay bar, where drag queens fought back over several days.

segments.title: Imperial Court System and drag balls
segments.summary: Jose Julio Sarria founded the Imperial Court System in San Francisco in the mid-1960s, a drag organization that held balls and later did philanthropic work. The drag balls became popular in the African American drag community, where sponsors ('fathers') mentor newcomers. Cyndi Lauper's Halloween party and her halfway house for kicked-out teens are mentioned. The hosts recommend the documentary Paris Is Burning.

segments.title: Becoming a drag queen: makeup, hands, tucking, breasts, names
segments.summary: The hosts describe the transformation: shaving, heavy makeup called beating your face, the hands (which Eltinge considered most important), tucking with tape or a gaff, optional silicone breasts that adhere to the body, and the tradition of playful drag names such as Madam Ovary and Della Coateessen.

segments.title: Drag performance work, Cockettes, Priscilla, and famous drag figures
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the Cockettes and Gore Vidal's review, drag performance formats such as lip-syncing and emceeing, Key West drag earnings, and Priscilla Queen of the Desert. They mention Mae West and Bert Savoy, Eddie Izzard, Danny La Rue, Doris Fish, Divine and Hairspray, Dame Edna, RuPaul, and Lady Bunny and Wigstock.

segments.title: Listener mail: Owen on post-graduation career advice
segments.summary: Owen, about to graduate from the University of Washington with a BA in Spanish and a BS in astronomy and physics, asks for advice. Josh suggests travel and following passions, and Chuck says that degrees often do not match jobs held later.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts invite listeners to learn more via the website, social media, and email, then close the show with a sponsor credit.
